# `Db.Store.Unsafe`

[Back to stdlib index](../stdlib.md)

Ipe.Db.Store.Unsafe — the raw, string-named query leaves and column-spec
builders for `Ipe.Db.Store`.

The safe `Ipe.Db.Store` surface names a column by an accessor literal
(`Store.eq .age 18`, `Store.primaryKey .id`), so the column is checked against
the row type at compile time. A raw-column store built by `Store.fromColumns`
has no such row type, so its columns can only be named by a bare string. Those
string-named query leaves (`eq`/`neq`/…) and column-spec builders
(`primaryKey`/`serial`/`defaultNow`/…) live here.

Importing this module discloses the `unsafe` capability program-wide. The
"unsafe" here is narrow: a column is named by an UNCHECKED string rather than a
compile-checked accessor. It is NOT an injection hatch — every column named by
these leaves is still validated against the store's own columns when the query
is built (`Store.where` / `Store.updateWhere` / `Store.deleteWhere` lower each
`Cond` through the same audited `SqlFragment` path, `Sql.column` for the
identifier and `Sql.param` for the value), so a column absent from the store is
a fail-closed `Err` and no value is ever interpolated.

## `eq`

```ipe
eq : String -> SqlValue -> Cond row
```

`eq col value` — the rows where `col` equals `value`. `value` binds as a
parameter; `col` is validated against the store's columns at query time.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.eq "id" (SqlString "u1"))

## `neq`

```ipe
neq : String -> SqlValue -> Cond row
```

`neq col value` — the rows where `col` differs from `value`.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.neq "status" (SqlString "deleted"))

## `gt`

```ipe
gt : String -> SqlValue -> Cond row
```

`gt col value` — the rows where `col` is greater than `value`.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.gt "age" (SqlInt 18))

## `gte`

```ipe
gte : String -> SqlValue -> Cond row
```

`gte col value` — the rows where `col` is greater than or equal to `value`.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.gte "age" (SqlInt 18))

## `lt`

```ipe
lt : String -> SqlValue -> Cond row
```

`lt col value` — the rows where `col` is less than `value`.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.lt "age" (SqlInt 65))

## `lte`

```ipe
lte : String -> SqlValue -> Cond row
```

`lte col value` — the rows where `col` is less than or equal to `value`.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.lte "age" (SqlInt 64))

## `like`

```ipe
like : String -> String -> Cond row
```

`like col pattern` — the rows where `col` matches the SQL `LIKE` `pattern`.
The pattern is bound as a parameter, never as SQL text. It is still a
pattern: `%` and `_` in it, including any that come from user text, are
wildcards. It is read under `ESCAPE '\'` on every engine, so `\%`, `\_` and
`\\` match `%`, `_` and `\` literally; a pattern ending in an unpaired `\` is
refused as a typed error.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.like "name" "al%")

## `isNull`

```ipe
isNull : String -> Cond row
```

`isNull col` — the rows where `col` is SQL `NULL`.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.isNull "deletedAt")

## `notNull`

```ipe
notNull : String -> Cond row
```

`notNull col` — the rows where `col` is not SQL `NULL`.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.notNull "email")

## `inList`

```ipe
inList : String -> List SqlValue -> Cond row
```

`inList col values` — the rows where `col` is one of `values`; each value
binds as a parameter. An EMPTY `values` matches no row (`(1 = 0)`), never an
ill-formed `IN ()`.

Example:

    Store.query store
        |> Store.where (Unsafe.inList "status" [ SqlString "active", SqlString "trial" ])

## `primaryKey`

```ipe
primaryKey : String -> Draft row -> Draft row
```

`primaryKey col draft` — mark the string-named `col` the primary key.

Example:

    Store.fromColumns "users" [ Store.textColumn "id" ]
        |> Result.map (Unsafe.primaryKey "id")
        |> Result.map Store.public

## `compositePrimaryKey`

```ipe
compositePrimaryKey : List String -> Draft row -> Draft row
```

`compositePrimaryKey cols draft` — make the string-named `cols`, in order,
one table-level primary key. Needs two or more distinct columns of the draft;
an empty or one-column list, a repeated or unknown column, or a draft that
already has a primary key is refused, fail-closed, when the schema is built.

Example:

    Store.fromColumns "memberships"
        [ Store.textColumn "org_id", Store.textColumn "user_id" ]
        |> Result.map (Unsafe.compositePrimaryKey [ "org_id", "user_id" ])
        |> Result.map Store.public

## `serial`

```ipe
serial : String -> Draft row -> Draft row
```

`serial col draft` — mark the string-named `col` DB-assigned (serial), so
`insert` omits it and the database generates it.

## `unique`

```ipe
unique : String -> Draft row -> Draft row
```

`unique col draft` — mark the string-named `col` unique.

## `defaultNow`

```ipe
defaultNow : String -> Draft row -> Draft row
```

`defaultNow col draft` — mark the string-named `col` DB-stamped with the
current time on insert, so `insert` omits it and the database stamps it.

## `touchOnUpdate`

```ipe
touchOnUpdate : String -> Draft row -> Draft row
```

`touchOnUpdate col draft` — mark the string-named `col` a DB-stamped
updated-at column, omitted from every client write so the database owns it.

## `defaultText`

```ipe
defaultText : String -> String -> Draft row -> Draft row
```

`defaultText col value draft` — give the string-named `col` a DB-level
`DEFAULT` of the text `value`. `value` is a fixed schema literal embedded in
the `CREATE TABLE` DDL: building the DDL rejects with a typed `Err` any
`value` carrying a control byte, newline, NUL, or backslash, and an accepted
`value` is single-quote escaped so it cannot break out of the literal under
any backend's string-quoting mode.

## `defaultInt`

```ipe
defaultInt : String -> Int -> Draft row -> Draft row
```

`defaultInt col value draft` — give the string-named `col` a DB-level
`DEFAULT` of the integer `value`. An integer renders as its own decimal
digits, so the emitted `DEFAULT` literal is always safe.
